name: CI

on:
  pull_request:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  workflow_dispatch:

permissions:
  contents: read

concurrency:
  group: ci-${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: ${{ github.event_name == 'pull_request' }}

# The e2e and WPT suites need more memory than a standard hosted runner has, so CI leaves them to
# local runs (AGENTS.md, "Running"); the Playwright lane runs on bazelflare's executors instead.
jobs:
  # One job, so the Rust crates compile once: the tests and the dev build share one Bazel output
  # tree, and the checks, the lint tests, the Rust host tests and the vitest suite one invocation.
  ci:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 120
    permissions:
      contents: read
      # Authenticates the job to bazelflare (bazel/bazelflare/credential-helper).
      id-token: write
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - id: setup
        uses: ./.github/actions/setup
        with:
          bazel-cache: "true"
          bazelflare: "true"
      - run: pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
      - run: bazel test --keep_going --test_output=errors //:check //:rust_lint //packages/core:host_tests //packages/engine:vitest
      - run: pnpm run build
      - name: Fail on generated drift
        run: git diff --exit-code
      - run: pnpm run format:check
      - run: pnpm run lint:js
      - run: bazel run //scripts:workspace_checks
      # Each spec boots an engine on a bazelflare executor, whose image holds the pinned Playwright
      # checkout. A fork's pull request has no bazelflare, so main runs the lane once it merges.
      - if: steps.setup.outputs.bazelflare == 'true'
        run: bazel test --keep_going --test_output=errors //tests/pw:specs //tests/pw:expectations_test
      - if: always()
        run: df -h /
      # Only main saves, so PR runs cannot evict main's entry from the 10 GB repository quota. Save
      # after a failure too: the actions that did finish are still valid cache entries.
      - if: >-
          !cancelled() && github.ref == 'refs/heads/main' && steps.setup.outputs.bazel-cache-key != ''
          && steps.setup.outputs.bazel-cache-hit != 'true'
        uses: actions/cache/save@v4
        with:
          path: ${{ steps.setup.outputs.bazel-cache-paths }}
          key: ${{ steps.setup.outputs.bazel-cache-key }}

# AGENTS.md

Guidance for contributors and coding agents. It records the constraints that are not obvious from
the code. Keep it short: state protocols and invariants as comments at the code that owns them,
point at code instead of restating it, and fix or delete anything here that becomes wrong.

## What this is

Kitesurf is a browser engine that runs on Cloudflare Workers. Each CDP WebSocket session runs in
one engine Worker. The engine parses HTML, runs page JS in per-page sub-isolates and renders frames
with Blitz (Stylo, Taffy, Parley and vello_cpu). The Rust code compiles to a few megabytes of
compressed WebAssembly behind a small TypeScript layer.

Kitesurf is a proof of concept and many parts are incomplete. Read the relevant code before
assuming standards compliance.

## Repository map

A pnpm monorepo. One line per package; read the code for details.

- `packages/engine/`: the engine Worker. CDP over WebSocket, PageScript orchestration and the wasm.
  `src/index.ts` routes, `src/cdp/` holds CDP methods, `src/eval/` the sub-isolate and subresource
  machinery, and `src/tty/` the terminal UA styles.
- `packages/page-script/`: the per-page runtime, bundled to a string and loaded through
  `env.LOADER`. Owns navigation, script execution and CDP DOM/eval routing. `state.ts` is the
  shared mutable state and holds `ksGlobal`, the package's typed view of `globalThis`
  (`PageScriptGlobals`, which extends dom-shim's `DomShimGlobals`). Declare a new page global
  there; computed keys go through `ksGlobalByKey`. Engine hooks go on the internals record
  instead (`KitesurfInternals` in `page-script/src/internal-state.ts`).
- `packages/dom-shim/`: the in-sandbox DOM (`buildDocument` and the Element, Node, Event and CSSOM
  classes), bundled to a string.
- `packages/core/`: Rust to wasm on Blitz. `DomHandle`, paint and screenshots, PDF, boa eval, the
  network provider and the `tty_*` terminal renderer. `pkg/` is staged by `pnpm run build`.
  The Rust crates form a Cargo workspace rooted at the repository's `Cargo.toml`.
- `packages/renderer-core/`: the renderer isolate's smaller wasm, the `SceneRasterizer` slice of
  core included with `#[path]`.
- `packages/page-renderer/`: the stateless raster worker. It pulls scenes from PageScript over the
  render port and owns the wasm resource cache.
- `packages/worker-script/`: the loaded worker that runs a page's `new Worker()`.
- `packages/script-gate/`: the shared script-execution policy (SRI, CSP `script-src`, JS MIME and
  `nosniff`, mixed content, the iframe sandbox capability set), so the engine and PageScript bundle
  one copy.
- `packages/jsrpc-types/`: type-only JSRPC contracts between the engine and its loaded workers.
  Both ends of a call import from here; do not redeclare a wire shape on one side.
- `packages/scene-host-wasm/`: the CLI's local scene rasterizer, staged into
  `packages/engine/public/rbi/`. The scene protocol is documented in `packages/engine/src/rbi.ts`.
- `packages/kitesurf-cli/`: the complete Rust terminal client, including Browser Run and OAuth
  through public APIs, with its own Cargo workspace and lockfile.
- `packages/engine/test/fixtures-worker/`: the fixtures Worker that serves `/__fixtures/*` in dev
  and tests only.
- `scripts/`: development and CI tooling, including the WPT runners, the lint rules and the
  vendored crate patch series. Each tool has a Bazel target in `scripts/BUILD.bazel`.
- `tests/`: the WPT allow-list, expectations and pinned revision. Bump the revision on purpose
  with `pnpm wpt:setup --update`; an unpinned corpus shows upstream changes as regressions.

## Architecture

Engine-wide invariants. The owning code carries the detail; keep these in sync with it.

- Runtime code generation (`Runtime.evaluate`, `eval`, `new Function`, computed `import()`) runs on
  boa inside the per-target PageScript isolate, in dev and production, never in the parent Worker.
  The loaded worker never gets a native-eval compatibility flag.
- The CDP WebSocket bounds the session. Per-connection state lives in `handleWebSocket`'s closure;
  no Durable Object holds it and nothing persists across connections.
- Each `Page.navigate` loads a fresh anonymous PageScript worker with `env.LOADER.load` and kills
  the previous one. Use `load()`, never a named `LOADER.get`.
- Wasm panics unwind (`packages/core/.cargo/config.toml`, symlinked into `renderer-core`), so the
  live DOM survives a panic. `scene-host-wasm` stays `abort`.
- The DevTools frontend is optional: `--config=devtools` stages Chrome's prebuilt one at
  `/inspector/`, deploys always include it, and `wrangler dev` falls back to Chrome's hosted one
  without it (`resolveInspectorBaseUrl`, README). Always send `devtoolsFrontendUrl`, or Chrome's
  **inspect** link does nothing.
- `/devtools/page/<id>` selects page mode, which never announces the page as a child target;
  Puppeteer must use `/devtools/browser`.
- CDP types come from `devtools-protocol`. Declare `Kitesurf.*` methods and extra fields in
  `cdp/protocol-extensions.ts`, and bump the root `pnpm.overrides` pin with the engine's version.
- A new target has a live `about:blank` document: `ensurePageScript` (`cdp/dom.ts`) starts a lazy
  isolate, because many clients evaluate without navigating.
- Layout is incremental. Work done at box construction needs explicit `CONSTRUCT_BOX` damage.
- Partial frames are composited in the renderer isolate (`SceneRasterizer`), so CDP clients
  never see one. The terminal scene stream is the exception; see `packages/engine/src/rbi.ts`.
- `history.pushState` stays in the document unless the navigate URL opts in with
  `?ks_refetch_on_pushstate=1`.

## Platform quirks with in-tree mitigations

Do not undo these.

- The sandbox ships a pure-JS `MessagePort`; page JS must never reach the native one.
- Every outbound request needs a deadline, and an ignored response body must be cancelled.

We do not shim single-subtest differences from the spec in the platform; we pin the test and report
upstream. Reproduce by running the snippet under `node` and under
`wrangler dev --compatibility-date=<date>`.

## Editing the in-isolate code

The loaded workers (`dom-shim`, `page-script`, `page-renderer`, `worker-script`) are TypeScript
bundled to strings that the engine passes to `env.LOADER.load`. All of them typecheck under
`pnpm run check`; do not add `@ts-nocheck`. Several page-script import specifiers
(`cloudflare:*`, `node:*`, `./wasm-glue.js`, `./core_bg.wasm`, `./dom-shim.js`) must survive
bundling unchanged: they are external and resolved by the loaded worker's module map.

Changes under those packages, and under `packages/core/`, need a restart of `pnpm run dev`, which
rebuilds them with Bazel; `packages/engine/src` hot-reloads.
`console.log` in the page isolate surfaces as CDP `Runtime.consoleAPICalled`.

## Building

Bazel builds and tests everything; the root `package.json` scripts are front ends to it. Add a
build step or check as a Bazel target, not as a pnpm script or a script that CI calls directly.
`pnpm run build` (`bazel run //packages/engine:dev_build`) copies the wasm, the loaded-worker
bundles and the RBI files into the source tree, where `wrangler dev` and tools outside Bazel read
them. The exceptions run cargo through rustup: the vendor patch workflow and the
memprof build (`pnpm run dev:memprof`).

## Vendored crate patches

Bazel applies `scripts/patches/<crate>-<version>/` to the registry source itself, so it builds only
committed patch files. Cargo builds patched crates (blitz, parley, taffy, stylo, selectors, boa and others) through the
root `Cargo.toml`'s `[patch.crates-io]`, pointing at `packages/core/target/vendor-patched/`.
`pnpm run vendor:apply` materializes each crate as a git repository: the registry source tagged
`vendor-base`, then the series from `scripts/patches/<crate>-<version>/` applied with `git am`.

To change a patch, iterate with `cargo check` from `packages/core/`, commit inside the vendor
tree, then run `pnpm run vendor:regen -- <crate>`; Bazel sees the change only after the regen.
Uncommitted or unregenerated work is lost when the tree is rebuilt, which any patch-file change or
`rm -rf packages/core/target` causes. Full workflow: [scripts/patches/README.md](scripts/patches/README.md).

## Running

```bash
pnpm install               # first time
pnpm run dev               # Bazel build, then wrangler dev on :8787
pnpm run check             # bazel test //:check, then the tracked-file checks
pnpm run test:e2e <file-substring>
pnpm run test:wpt --filter <substring>
pnpm run test:playwright --filter <substring>
pnpm run test:puppeteer --filter <substring>   # after pnpm run pptr:setup
```

Use an explicit `KITESURF_PORT` or `--port` when other engines may be running, and stop only the
`wrangler` and `workerd` processes you started.

- **Deploying:** `pnpm run deploy [wrangler deploy args]` builds with `--config=devtools` and
  uploads `:dist` and the assets unbundled (`scripts/engine-deploy.mjs`) to wrangler's account.
  `pnpm run deploy:preview` does the same with `wrangler versions upload`, which moves no traffic.
  `packages/engine/wrangler.jsonc` stays a template with no account or routes. Agents never deploy.
- **Tracing:** send a `traceparent` header (or a bare trace id in it) with `pnpm dev:tracing` running.
- **WPT:** `test:wpt` starts, health-checks and stops its own engines every `--batch-size` tests.
  It refuses to start if a port in its range is taken. `-j N` runs N engines and uses ports
  `port` to `port+2N-1`. It fails on any deviation from `tests/wpt-expectations.json`, including
  unexpected passes; rebaseline with `--update-expectations` in a separate commit. Tests with
  variants are enrolled once per variant.
- **testdriver:** `test_driver.click`, `send_keys` and `Actions().send()` dispatch real CDP input.
  Other actions keep upstream's "not implemented" error, and `in_automation` stays `false`.

## Conventions

### Branches and commits

- Branch from an up-to-date `origin/main` before the first edit; never commit on `main`.
- Read `git log --oneline` first. Use a one-line imperative summary of about 70 characters, and a
  body that explains why.
- Keep commits atomic: one reason per commit. Squash work-in-progress commits before review.
- Sign off every commit (`git commit -s`); see [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md).
- Do not commit plans, findings, inventories or scratch reproductions. `PLAN.md`, `TODO.md` and
  `FINDINGS.md` are gitignored for that purpose. Keep durable findings as a code comment.
- Agents do not push; leave that to the person they work for.

### Code style

- Put durable engine behavior (layout, geometry, parsing, traversal, other stateful work) in
  Rust. Keep TypeScript to API wiring, lifecycle and callback delivery, unless the logic owns
  page-realm semantics or Rust cannot observe the state it needs.
- TypeScript shim classes use explicit getters and setters, with closure-scoped helpers for shared
  state.
- In Rust, pair `borrow()` and `borrow_mut()` with an explicit `drop()` before returning, and
  validate node ids before passing them to Blitz.
- Comment blocks have at most four lines of at most 100 columns and no blank interior lines
  (`scripts/lint/comment-policy.mjs` lists the exemptions).
- Hand-written type declarations go in `.ts` files, never `.d.ts`: `skipLibCheck` would skip
  them. A declaration for a module supplied at runtime (`./wasm-glue.js`, `./__ks_*.js`) uses
  `export declare` and the `@ks-declaration-twin` marker, which fails the build if it is bundled.
- Every tracked TypeScript file must be covered by a typechecked tsconfig, and every tsconfig must
  set `types` (`scripts/check-ts-coverage.mjs`).
- In bundled packages, write a function inside a block as `const f = function …`. esbuild hoists
  block-level function declarations out of their block under `alwaysStrict`.

### Tests

- Never run a full suite unless asked; the runners are slow and memory-hungry. CI runs the
  Playwright lane, but not the e2e or WPT lanes. Before reporting work complete, run
  `pnpm run check` and the smallest relevant e2e subset. Uncaught workerd errors fail a run even
  if assertions pass.
- Do not put `--` before test arguments; pnpm forwards it and the runners misread it.
- Prefer a hermetic e2e test (`packages/engine/test/e2e/**.e2e.test.ts`) over a script or demo.
  They boot the engine in-process with `@cloudflare/vitest-plugin` and drive it over CDP. Give each
  test its own markup with `setContent` (`test/e2e/set-content.ts`); add a `/__fixtures/*` route
  only when the page needs a real origin.
- For a WPT failure: reproduce the smallest failing unit in a scratch script, fix it, rerun the
  affected subtree with `--filter`, rebaseline in a separate commit, then add a hermetic e2e test.

## Out of scope unless asked

- Running iframe JS in the parent isolate. Iframes render, and script-free same-origin
  `contentDocument` supports a partial mutation subset.
- Service and shared workers. Dedicated workers work, except module workers and `importScripts`.
- A live SVG DOM. Inline `<svg>` is painted from a usvg snapshot that DOM mutations refresh;
  SVG-specific interfaces are `Element` aliases.
- Synchronous XHR. workerd has no way to block the JS thread on network I/O.
- A fake `crypto.subtle`; Workers provide the real one.
- WebGL, WebGPU, WebAudio, WebRTC, MediaStream and anti-bot fingerprinting.
- Persistent storage across navigations or connections, and WebDriver; Kitesurf speaks CDP.

![Kitesurf logo](.github/assets/kitesurf_logo.png)

# Kitesurf

Kitesurf is an experimental browser engine that runs on Cloudflare Workers. It
parses HTML, applies CSS, runs page JavaScript, and renders screenshots without
Chrome or a browser container.

Kitesurf speaks the [Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP)](https://chromedevtools.github.io/devtools-protocol/),
so you can use it with CDP clients such as Puppeteer.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> Kitesurf requires Cloudflare Dynamic Workers to create isolated workers for
> pages. Dynamic Workers are part of the [Workers Paid plan](https://developers.cloudflare.com/dynamic-workers/pricing/).
> Local development uses `wrangler dev`. A Cloudflare Workers Paid plan is
> required to run Kitesurf on Cloudflare.

## Requirements

- [Bazelisk](https://github.com/bazelbuild/bazelisk), installed as `bazel`.
  Bazel builds everything. It downloads the pinned Bazel, Rust toolchains,
  wasm-bindgen, and binaryen itself.
- Node.js 22 or newer
- pnpm 9.15.4, which the repository pins in `package.json`
- On macOS, GNU tar (`brew install gnu-tar`)
- Rust through [rustup](https://rustup.rs/), only for editing the vendored
  crate patches. `rust-toolchain.toml` pins the same nightly that Bazel uses.

Install pnpm separately if it is not already available:

```bash
npm install --global pnpm@9.15.4
```

## Build and run locally

Clone the repository and install its dependencies:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/cloudflare/kitesurf.git
cd kitesurf
pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
```

Build and start the local engine:

```bash
pnpm run dev
```

The engine listens on `http://127.0.0.1:8787`. Visit
`http://127.0.0.1:8787/health` to confirm that it is running.

The root URL shows the landing page. It has a form to open a URL in Chrome
DevTools, example pages, and the CDP endpoints for agents and other clients.
See [Use Chrome DevTools](#use-chrome-devtools).

`pnpm run dev` builds the WebAssembly modules and the page and renderer bundles
with Bazel, then starts `wrangler dev`. The first build compiles the Rust core
and its vendored crates, which takes a while; later builds reuse Bazel's cache.

Set `KITESURF_PORT` when port `8787` is already in use:

```bash
KITESURF_PORT=8799 pnpm run dev
```

## Connect with Puppeteer

Install `puppeteer-core` in the project that will control Kitesurf. Then connect
to the browser WebSocket endpoint:

```js
import puppeteer from "puppeteer-core";

const browser = await puppeteer.connect({
  browserWSEndpoint: "ws://127.0.0.1:8787/devtools/browser",
});

const page = await browser.newPage();
await page.goto("https://example.com/");
await page.screenshot({ path: "page.png" });

await browser.disconnect();
```

Use the port from `KITESURF_PORT` if you selected a different port. HTTP
discovery is available at `http://127.0.0.1:8787/json/version`.

## Use Chrome DevTools

With `pnpm run dev`, open `http://127.0.0.1:8787/` in Chrome. Enter a URL to
inspect, or select one of the example pages. DevTools opens in the tab on that
page. To go to DevTools directly, open
`http://127.0.0.1:8787/?url=https://example.com`, or
`http://127.0.0.1:8787/?inspect=1` for a blank page.

If you built the bundled frontend, `pnpm run dev` serves it from the engine's
own origin. See
[Use the bundled DevTools frontend](#use-the-bundled-devtools-frontend).
Otherwise, the DevTools frontend comes from
`chrome-devtools-frontend.appspot.com`, the build that Google hosts for Chrome.
The hosted frontend has these limits:

- The first time it connects, Chrome asks whether
  `chrome-devtools-frontend.appspot.com` can access apps on this device. Select
  **Allow**.
- If you block this access, DevTools says that the WebSocket disconnected. To
  allow it again, click the site information icon to the left of the address.
  Then allow the access and reconnect DevTools.
- The frontend can connect only to `127.0.0.1`. Thus it does not work with a
  deployed engine.

You can also use `chrome://inspect`:

1. Open `chrome://inspect/#devices` in Chrome. Type or paste it into the address
   bar because web pages cannot link to it.
2. Select **Discover network targets**.
3. Select **Configure...** and add `127.0.0.1:8787`.
4. Under **Remote Target**, select **inspect** next to **kitesurf**.
5. Enter a page URL in the address bar above the screencast.

Use the port from `KITESURF_PORT` when you select a different local port. Chrome
discovers targets with plain HTTP and WebSocket connections. The `chrome://inspect`
workflow cannot reach an HTTPS engine. Use it with a local engine instead.

Kitesurf provides a CDP endpoint, not a full Chrome implementation. Some Chrome
DevTools features do not work yet. We are working to add more support over time.
Puppeteer and other CDP clients can connect to
`ws://127.0.0.1:8787/devtools/browser`.

### Use the bundled DevTools frontend

Kitesurf can serve the Chrome DevTools frontend from its own origin. Then
DevTools works without the hosted frontend, its permission prompt and the
`127.0.0.1` limit. A deployed engine always uses this copy. The frontend is the
prebuilt build that Google publishes for Chromium. The default build does not
include it.

#### Build the frontend

The `--config=devtools` Bazel option adds the frontend to the build. The first
build with it downloads the frontend (about 250 MB). Bazel keeps the download
in its cache for later builds.

To build the frontend once, run this command from the repository root:

```bash
bazel run --config=devtools //packages/engine:dev_build
```

To include the frontend in every local build, add the option to
`.bazelrc.user`. Git ignores this file. Then `pnpm run build` and
`pnpm run dev` include the frontend.

```bash
echo 'common --config=devtools' >> .bazelrc.user
```

The build copies the frontend to `packages/engine/public/inspector/`. Git
ignores this directory. A build without the option removes it. To turn the
frontend off, remove the line from `.bazelrc.user`.

#### Run the frontend locally

1. Build the frontend as described above.
2. Start the engine with `pnpm run dev`. The engine serves the bundled frontend
   when the build includes it, and the hosted frontend when it does not.
3. Open `http://127.0.0.1:8787/` in Chrome. Enter a URL to inspect, or select
   one of the example pages. DevTools opens in the tab on that page.

To start on a page, open `http://127.0.0.1:8787/?url=https://example.com`.

#### Rebuild the frontend

Use the smallest step that fixes the problem:

- To copy the frontend files again, delete the copy and build again:

  ```bash
  rm -rf packages/engine/public/inspector
  bazel run --config=devtools //packages/engine:dev_build
  ```

- To extract the archive again, for example after you change
  `bazel/devtools_frontend.BUILD`, fetch it again and then build:

  ```bash
  bazel fetch --force --repo=@devtools_frontend --config=devtools
  bazel run --config=devtools //packages/engine:dev_build
  ```

  Bazel extracts the archive from its cache. To download the archive again
  from Google, add `--repository_cache=` to the `bazel fetch` command.

Do not use `bazel clean --expunge` for this. It also removes the WebAssembly
build and the rest of the Bazel cache.

#### Update the frontend version

Two pins select the frontend version:

- `DEVTOOLS_FRONTEND_REV` and the values after it in `MODULE.bazel` select the
  bundled frontend. The comment above them tells you how to select a new
  snapshot.
- `KITESURF_INSPECTOR_FALLBACK_URL` in the `local` environment of
  `packages/engine/wrangler.jsonc` selects the hosted frontend. Use the
  Chrome commit that
  `https://chromiumdash.appspot.com/fetch_version?version=<chrome-version>`
  returns in `hashes.chromium`.

Keep the two pins on the same Chrome version. After you change
`MODULE.bazel`, the next build downloads the new archive.

## Build and test

The pnpm scripts are front ends to Bazel:

```bash
pnpm run build                    # bazel run //packages/engine:dev_build
pnpm run check                    # type checks, bundles, and repository checks
pnpm run test:unit                # engine vitest and Rust host tests
pnpm run test:e2e <file-substring>
pnpm run format:check             # oxfmt; pnpm run format rewrites the same files
pnpm run format:rust              # format Rust with Bazel's pinned rustfmt
pnpm run lint                     # oxlint, the custom lint rules, and Rust lint
```

The Rust formatter rewrites tracked and non-ignored untracked files, excluding
paths in `.oxfmtrc.json`.

`pnpm run build` copies the Bazel-built WebAssembly, bundles, and RBI files into
the source tree, where `wrangler dev` reads them. Other targets run directly,
for example `bazel test //tests/e2e:gate` for the full e2e suite. Another Bazel
workspace can depend on this repository as a module.

## Technology stack

Kitesurf combines several open-source Rust projects:

- [Blitz](https://github.com/DioxusLabs/blitz) provides HTML parsing, the DOM,
  layout, and painting. It is licensed under `MIT OR Apache-2.0`.
- [Stylo](https://github.com/servo/stylo) provides CSS parsing, cascading, and
  computed styles. It is licensed under `MPL-2.0`.
- [Boa](https://github.com/boa-dev/boa) runs page JavaScript inside WebAssembly.
  It is licensed under `Unlicense OR MIT`.
- [Linebender](https://linebender.org/) libraries provide text layout and 2D
  graphics, including [Parley](https://github.com/linebender/parley),
  [Vello](https://github.com/linebender/vello),
  [Kurbo](https://github.com/linebender/kurbo), and
  [Peniko](https://github.com/linebender/peniko). These libraries are licensed
  under `Apache-2.0 OR MIT`.
- [Krilla](https://github.com/LaurenzV/krilla) generates PDF output. It is
  licensed under `MIT OR Apache-2.0`.

Kitesurf patches its Rust dependencies. The patch series are in
[`scripts/patches/`](scripts/patches/), and Bazel applies them itself.

## Cloudflare deployment

> [!WARNING]
> Do not deploy Kitesurf without authentication in front of it. Use
> [Cloudflare Access](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/configuration/routing/workers-dev/#manage-access-to-workersdev)
> (Cloudflare Zero Trust) or another authentication layer. The engine has no
> authentication of its own. A person who has the URL can:
>
> - Open DevTools and browse the web through your engine.
> - Connect Puppeteer and other CDP clients to it.
> - Send outbound requests that come from your Cloudflare account.
> - Use CPU time and Dynamic Workers that your account pays for.
>
> The `workers.dev` URL is public by default. Its name follows a predictable
> pattern: `kitesurf.<your-subdomain>.workers.dev`.

To deploy the engine as a Worker on your Cloudflare account:

1. Deploy the engine. Run the command from the repository root. In a package
   directory, use `pnpm -w run deploy`.

   ```bash
   pnpm run deploy
   ```

2. Protect the Worker URL with Cloudflare Access immediately. Follow
   [Manage access to `workers.dev`](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/configuration/routing/workers-dev/#manage-access-to-workersdev).
   For a custom domain or route, protect it with a
   [self-hosted Access application](https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/applications/configure-apps/self-hosted-public-app/).
3. Open the Worker URL in Chrome. Access asks you to sign in. Then the landing
   page opens. Enter a URL to open it in DevTools.

Between steps 1 and 2, the engine is public. To prevent this gap, turn on Access
for all Workers in the account before you deploy. The `workers.dev` page in
step 2 tells you how.

The command builds the engine with Bazel and uploads it with Wrangler. Wrangler
uses the account of `wrangler login`, or `CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID` and
`CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN`. The command sends other arguments to `wrangler deploy`,
for example `--name <worker-name>`. Without `--name`, the Worker name is
`kitesurf`.

To build the deploy without an upload, run `pnpm run deploy --dry-run`.

To upload a version without sending traffic to it, run `pnpm run deploy:preview`.
The command runs `wrangler versions upload`. If the Worker has Version URLs
turned on, Wrangler prints the URL of the new version. Version URLs are public
too. Protect them with Access as well. Follow
[Manage access to Version URLs](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/versions-and-deployments/version-urls/#manage-access-to-version-urls).

The deploy always builds with `--config=devtools`, so it includes the Chrome
DevTools frontend. You do not need `.bazelrc.user` for it. The first deploy
downloads the frontend, as the first local build does. The deploy sets
`KITESURF_INSPECTOR_BASE_URL` to `/inspector/inspector.html`. To use a different
frontend, add `--var KITESURF_INSPECTOR_BASE_URL:<url>` to the command.

DevTools loads from the Worker's own origin, so its WebSocket sends the Access
cookie. A DevTools frontend on another origin cannot connect through Access.

### Connect a CDP client through Access

Access blocks a CDP client that has no browser session. To connect Puppeteer:

1. Create an
   [Access service token](https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/service-credentials/service-tokens/).
2. Add a policy with the **Service Auth** action that allows this token.
3. Send the token headers with the WebSocket connection:

   ```js
   const browser = await puppeteer.connect({
     browserWSEndpoint: "wss://<worker-host>/devtools/browser",
     headers: {
       "CF-Access-Client-Id": process.env.CF_ACCESS_CLIENT_ID,
       "CF-Access-Client-Secret": [REDACTED],
     },
   });
   ```

Keep the service token secret. The token gives the same access as a signed-in
user.

The engine configuration includes a Worker Loader binding. Kitesurf uses this
binding to start a separate worker for each page and renderer. Cloudflare
Dynamic Workers provide this capability, and they require the Workers Paid plan.
See the [Dynamic Workers pricing](https://developers.cloudflare.com/dynamic-workers/pricing/)
documentation before planning a Cloudflare deployment.

## Scope

kitesurf renders pages written by others, so these classes of bug are in
scope:

- Escape from a page's isolate into the engine or the host runtime.
- Data that crosses origins or sessions.
- Network requests that a session's configuration does not allow.
- Authentication or authorization bypass on the engine's HTTP or CDP
  endpoints.

The engine has no authentication or rate limit of its own. Anyone who can reach
it can open sessions and make it fetch arbitrary URLs, so an embedder must
supply admission through `EngineHost.admit` or put a gateway in front of it.

    environment:

    ports:
      # Loopback only: the collector is unauthenticated and stores page text
      # and request URLs. Docker publishes 0.0.0.0 when the host IP is omitted.
      - "127.0.0.1:4318:4318"
      - "127.0.0.1:16686:16686"

# Kitesurf CLI Kitesurf opens websites in your terminal. It receives scenes over CDP and renders them locally using Kitty graphics; use `--mode=ansi` for selectable text in any terminal. ## How it works ![End-to-end flow from website through the engine and CLI to the terminal](architecture.svg) The engine sends drawing commands over CDP. The CLI replays them with a downloaded Wasm rasterizer, displays Kitty graphics or ANSI text, and acknowledges each scene so the engine can send the next one. By default, CDP connects through the official Browser Run API with `browser=kitesurf`. After connecting, the CLI asks that engine for its scene-host manifest over CDP. On a cache miss it downloads the matching Wasm in chunks of up to 4 MiB, verifies its size and SHA-256, and caches it by hash. A cache hit only needs the manifest. This also applies to playground and direct/local connections, so each engine supplies its own rasterizer. Scene wire-version checks remain in place before replay. In Browser Run mode, built-in fonts come from `https://kitesurf.dev/rbi/fonts/` without API or Cloudflare Access credentials. Direct connections, including the playground, fetch `/rbi/fonts/` from the connected engine's origin and send `CF_ACCESS_TOKEN` if set. Font redirects must stay on that origin. Page-provided fonts still travel in CDP resource batches. Built-in fonts are cached on disk in `$XDG_CACHE_HOME/kitesurf/fonts/`, or `~/.cache/kitesurf/fonts/` when `XDG_CACHE_HOME` is unset. Each entry stores the font bytes, their SHA-256 and size, and the server's ETag. On a later run, the CLI checks the local bytes and sends `If-None-Match`; an HTTP 304 reuses those bytes without downloading the font again. A changed font or damaged cache entry triggers a full download. Responses without an ETag are downloaded again on the next run. Cache write failures do not prevent rendering; `--debug` reports them. Individual fonts remain capped at 16 MiB. The engine must support `Kitesurf.getSceneHostManifest` and `Kitesurf.readSceneHost`. Deploy that support before installing this CLI version. An older engine produces an upgrade error; the CLI does not fall back to a different environment's rasterizer. The HTTP scene-host routes remain available for older clients. In graphics mode, localized changes arrive as damage-rectangle scenes. The downloaded rasterizer composites them into a retained viewport, so the CLI replays only the changed region. It still displays a complete image using ordinary Kitty image placement, including on Ghostty. Navigation, resize, or a missing base frame triggers a full scene. Older rasterizers and ANSI mode use full scenes. For example, `

Hello

` uses Kitesurf's built-in Noto Sans font even though the page provides no font file. The CDP resource batch identifies it as `/fonts/NotoSans.ttf`. If the rasterizer needs it, the CLI fetches `/rbi/fonts/NotoSans.ttf` from the font origin described above and supplies the bytes to the Wasm. A font loaded by the page with `@font-face` instead travels in the CDP resource batch. The separately downloaded `scene_host.wasm` is the rasterizer program, not a bundle of fonts. [Mermaid source](architecture.mmd) · [PNG](architecture.png) ## Install From a checkout of this repository, with Rust 1.96 or later installed: ```sh cargo install --path packages/kitesurf-cli --locked ``` This installs `kitesurf` in Cargo's bin directory (usually `~/.cargo/bin`). On Linux the build compiles its TLS stack (Rustls on aws-lc-rs) with the system C compiler and trusts the system certificate store. The credential store integration builds vendored D-Bus and OpenSSL dependencies. macOS and Windows use the platform's TLS. The Rust package also exposes the `kitesurf_playback` library. `play` accepts a connected `CdpSocket`, validated `PlaybackOptions`, and a `FontSource` containing the font origin and its HTTP client. The CLI handles Browser Run authentication; `PlaybackOptions::new` enforces the 1-60 FPS limit. ## Run Open a page through Browser Run: ```sh kitesurf https://example.com/ ``` Without a saved login, the CLI starts OAuth automatically and opens the requested page after you sign in. Run `kitesurf login` to sign in separately or select a different account. Both `kitesurf --help` and `kitesurf login --help` show the full usage and authentication instructions. Login opens your browser for Cloudflare consent and listens on `http://localhost:8976/oauth/callback` for up to five minutes. Choose the account(s) to authorize, then select an account in the terminal if more than one is available. Set `CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID` before login to select a specific authorized account without the terminal prompt. The selected account, access token, refresh token, and expiry are saved in the OS credential store: Keychain on macOS, Credential Manager on Windows, or Secret Service on Linux. Linux login needs an unlocked Secret Service keyring and a D-Bus session. Tokens nearing expiry refresh before a new connection. If the token endpoint rejects the refresh grant (`invalid_grant`) or no refresh token was issued, the CLI starts OAuth login again and continues opening the requested page after you sign in. Network errors, timeouts, and other token-endpoint failures keep the saved credentials and return an error so you can try again. If Browser Run rejects the saved OAuth token with HTTP 401, the CLI starts OAuth login automatically, retries the connection once with the new credentials, and opens the requested page. A failed login or rejected retry returns an error. Explicit API tokens and direct engine connections do not start OAuth login. `kitesurf logout` revokes the tokens and removes the saved login. If remote revocation fails, it still removes the local login and tells you to revoke the authorization in the Cloudflare dashboard. For CI or terminals without a credential store, use an API token with `Browser Rendering - Edit` permission: ```sh export CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID="" export KITESURF_API_TOKEN="" kitesurf https://example.com/ ``` `KITESURF_API_TOKEN` takes precedence over saved OAuth credentials and requires an explicit account ID. `CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN` is ignored, so exported Wrangler deployment credentials do not override your Kitesurf login. Neither Browser Run tokens nor saved OAuth credentials are sent to the playground asset host. To use the public playground without Cloudflare credentials: ```sh kitesurf --playground https://example.com/ ``` For selectable text, use `kitesurf --mode=ansi https://example.com/`. ### OAuth application setup The CLI defaults to public client ID `c9007ad1-f329-4bc0-93b5-931f78e8e64e`, with Authorization Code and Refresh Token grants, PKCE `S256`, token authentication method `none`, and the exact redirect URI `http://localhost:8976/oauth/callback`. No client secret is shipped or required. Set `KITESURF_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID` to use another registered client, such as staging: ```sh KITESURF_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID="" kitesurf https://example.com/ ``` The override applies to login, token exchange, refresh, and logout. Saved credentials are separate for each client ID; use the same override when browsing or logging out of that client. Switching to a client without saved credentials starts OAuth automatically. Each client must allow the redirect URI, grants, and scopes described here. Configure the client's required scopes to allow `browser-rendering.write` (Browser Run Write) and `account-settings.read` (Account Settings Read, for `GET /client/v4/accounts`). Enable the `refresh_token` grant alongside `authorization_code`; Cloudflare automatically allows the `offline_access` protocol scope when refresh tokens are enabled. It is not a product scope in the scope picker. Login explicitly requests both product scopes and `offline_access`. Registration defines the allowed permissions; omitting the authorization request's `scope` parameter produces an empty consent list. Verify consent and a Browser Run session after registration changes. A private client can only be authorized by members of its owning account. Public distribution requires public client visibility and publisher domain verification. An account administrator can also block new public OAuth grants. ## Running locally Start the Kitesurf engine from the repo root, then run the client in another terminal: ```sh KITESURF_PORT=8799 KITESURF_INSPECTOR_PORT=9239 pnpm run dev KITESURF_SERVER=http://127.0.0.1:8799 kitesurf https://example.com/ ``` Running `kitesurf` without a URL shows command-line help. Local Kitty mode needs a Kitty-graphics terminal such as Ghostty; ANSI mode works without one. ## Options | Option | Description | | -------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | `--playground` | Connect directly to kitesurf.dev. Cannot be combined with `KITESURF_SERVER`. | | `--mode=kitty\|ansi` | Choose Kitty graphics (default) or ANSI text. | | `--fps N` | Cap the scene rate (1–60; default 60). | | `--seconds N` | Stop replay after N seconds and print measurements. | | `--no-display` | Measure replay without drawing to the terminal. | | `--debug` (or `--verbose`) | Log connection, artifact/cache, font download and scene-stream events to stderr. With the full-screen display, later events print after it closes; use `--no-display --debug` for live logs. | | `--version` | Print the CLI version. | | `-h`, `--help` | Show command-line help. | ## Environment variables | Variable | Description | | -------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | `CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID` | Browser Run account ID. Overrides the saved OAuth account; required when using an explicit API token. Also selects an account during login. | | `KITESURF_API_TOKEN` | Browser Run bearer token, used instead of saved OAuth credentials. Sent only on the API WebSocket handshake. `CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN` is ignored. | | `KITESURF_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID` | Override the official OAuth client ID, for example for staging. Saved OAuth credentials are separate per client ID. | | `KITESURF_SERVER` | Direct engine URL, bypassing Browser Run and OAuth. Remote engines require HTTPS; HTTP is allowed on loopback for local development. | | `CF_ACCESS_TOKEN` | Cloudflare Access token for a direct engine's WebSocket handshake and font requests. Ignored in Browser Run mode. Font redirects must stay on the engine origin. | | `KITESURF_KITTY_PNG` | Use PNG instead of raw RGBA files in local Ghostty; useful for comparing rendering speed. | For example, to use an engine behind Cloudflare Access, run this once: ```sh cloudflared access login -app=https://kitesurf.example.com ``` And then this every time: ```sh CF_ACCESS_TOKEN=[REDACTED] access token -app=https://kitesurf.example.com) \ KITESURF_SERVER=https://kitesurf.example.com \ kitesurf https://example.com/ ``` The stats bar is on by default. Press Ctrl-B to toggle it, or Ctrl-C to exit. Its `acct` value is the server's accounted memory across the engine, page isolates, and renderer; it omits untracked allocations and is not the Worker's total memory use.

# Patches

**Vendor crate patches** — deltas against library crates that cargo
links into the wasm build. The provenance table lists all patched
crates.

Each crate's delta is a **git-format-patch series** in
`scripts/patches/<crate>-<version>/` — numbered `0001-*.patch`,
`0002-*.patch`, … applied in filename order. Every patch is a real
git commit (author, date, subject, message body), so `git log` in the
materialised tree reads like the crate's local history and each
logical change is reviewable on its own.

Each patch carries its real author. Only the materialiser's own
`vendor-base` commit and the committer field use the synthetic vendor
identity.

Materialised at build time by `scripts/get-patched-vendor-crates.mjs`
into `packages/core/target/vendor-patched/<crate>-<version>/`, where
the repo-root `Cargo.toml`'s `[patch.crates-io]` block picks them up
(cargo only honors patch tables in the workspace root manifest).

Historical: this directory previously held one monolithic
`<crate>-<version>.patch` per crate (and before that, a build-tool
patch against `wasm-bindgen-cli`, obsoleted by wasm-bindgen 0.2.122).
The monolithic patches were folded into each series' `0001` baseline
commit; new changes land as separate commits on top.

See the repo-root `Cargo.toml`'s `[patch.crates-io]` block for the
library wiring and `AGENTS.md` for the architectural background.

---

## How it works

Each series applies against the **registry tarball** for the named
crate at the named version. The pristine tarball is whatever
`~/.cargo/registry/src/index.crates.io-*/<crate>-<version>/`
contains after `cargo info --locked --registry crates-io <crate>@<version>`.

`scripts/get-patched-vendor-crates.mjs` materialises each crate into
`packages/core/target/vendor-patched/<crate>-<version>/` as a **real
git repo**:

1. copy the registry source verbatim (`chmod -R u+w` — registry
   sources are read-only),
2. `git init`; commit everything as the base commit, tagged
   **`vendor-base`** (fixed synthetic identity + epoch-ish date, so
   the base commit is byte-deterministic across machines),
3. `git am` the series — one commit per patch, preserving each
   patch's author, date, and message,
4. record the series sha8 in a `.patch-sha8` marker so subsequent
   runs no-op until any patch in the series changes.

Bazel does not read these trees. Its `patched_crate` repository rule
(`bazel/rust/crates.bzl`) applies the committed `.patch` files to the
registry source itself, so the trees are only for editing patches and
for direct `cargo` builds from `packages/core/`, which work as long as
the materialiser has run at least once since the last series change.

The materialised trees live under `target/` (gitignored), so nothing
patched (and no nested `.git`) ends up committed. Only the `.patch`
files in this directory carry the delta.

All plumbing git invocations run with `GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL=/dev/null` /
`GIT_CONFIG_SYSTEM=/dev/null`, so user config (gpg signing, autocrlf,
`format.*`) can't leak into materialisation or regenerated patches.

## What each series carries

**The commit messages are the documentation** — read them directly:

```bash
head -40 scripts/patches/<crate>-<version>/*.patch   # From/Subject/body
# or, after materialising:
git -C packages/core/target/vendor-patched/<crate>-<version> log
```

One-line orientation (see each series' patches for the full why):

- **parley** — inline-span box decorations (padding/border/background/
  radius on text spans) + the per-line span-fragment sidecar the
  painter consumes; tab-size stops, per-paragraph `dir=auto`,
  `first_strong_direction`, `truncate_lines` for line-clamp.
- **parley_engine** — the engine halves of the base-direction and tab
  patches: parley 0.12 moved analysis, bidi and shaping into this crate.
- **blitz-dom** — stylo→parley decoration extraction, driving stylo's
  relative-selector invalidator so `:has()` invalidates, + assorted layout
  and robustness fixes (placeholder polyfill, float paint-order gate,
  inline metrics/positioning, font loading, `clear_style_snapshots`
  cascade-panic recovery, …).
- **blitz-html** — the XHTML sniff stops at the first non-root start
  tag outside comments and quoted literals, so text later on a minified
  one-line page cannot route it to the XML parser (`core/src/dom/scan.rs`
  mirrors the rule).
- **blitz-paint** — paints the span-fragment decorations; canvas
  background propagation; SVG background-repeat tiling; and the
  `begin_part`/`end_part` markers a consumer needs to know what a rect
  is FOR (see `anyrender` below).
- **anyrender** — `PaintScene::begin_part`/`end_part`, defaulted to
  no-ops, so the painter can name which part of which element it is
  about to draw instead of the consumer inferring it back from
  geometry, plus the form-control state (`checked`) that pixels cannot
  reveal. Consumed by the scene wire (`scene_record.rs`). Also
  `push_clip_path`/`pop_clip_path`, defaulted to a clip layer, so a
  backend can clip each draw instead of compositing a group.
- **anyrender_vello_cpu** - implements `push_clip_path` with vello_cpu's
  clip paths. The scene replayer uses it for whole-pixel rect clips,
  where it gives the same pixels as a clip layer without the extra
  layer composite (`core/src/paint/scene_replay.rs`). Also skips premultiplying
  opaque images, such as canvas frames.
- **taffy** — layout fixes for floats, grid sizing, absolute grid
  placement, a host rounding step, and lazy per-node cache allocation.
- **stylo_taffy** — map anchor-dependent values to their fallback (or
  the property's initial value) instead of panicking.
- **ratatui-image** — feature-gates the terminal-capability query
  (`query`, default-on) so the crate builds for wasm at all: rustix is
  declared unconditionally for `cfg(not(windows))`, and its errno dep
  hard-errors on `target_os = "unknown"`. Upstreamable as-is.
- **stylo** — `@page` descriptors for the servo build, which omits Gecko-only longhands,
  unstyled-snapshot invalidation tolerance, and a finished
  animation keeping its `animation-fill-mode: forwards` contribution.
- **boa_ast / boa_parser / boa_interner / boa_gc / boa_engine** —
  load-bearing fixes for the eval-less runtime path (runtime eval always runs on boa),
  plus interpreter speed and memory work (each patch's message carries
  its measurements).
- **jpeg-encoder** — wasm SIMD128 color conversion and fused block
  sampling, DCT, quantization and zigzag, plus portable Huffman writer
  speedups, plus even-pixel-only chroma conversion on 4:2:0 rows, for
  screencast JPEG encoding. Output stays byte-identical
  to upstream.
- **vello_common** — consecutive fills of one gradient share one colour
  lookup table, so the thousands of tiles blitz-paint draws for a
  repeating gradient do not each allocate their own.

## Editing vendor source and regenerating the series

The vendor-patched tree is a real git repo whose history is
`vendor-base` (pristine upstream) + one commit per patch. Iterate with
plain git:

```bash
# One-time (or after a series change): materialise the trees.
pnpm run vendor:apply

# Edit, e.g.:
$EDITOR packages/core/target/vendor-patched/blitz-dom-0.3.0-beta.4/src/document.rs

# Iterate: cargo picks up edits in place. Bazel does not, until the regen.
(cd packages/core && cargo check --target wasm32-unknown-unknown)

# Once the fix is good, COMMIT it in the vendor tree. The commit
# message becomes the patch — subject + body explaining why.
git -C packages/core/target/vendor-patched/blitz-dom-0.3.0-beta.4 add -A
git -C packages/core/target/vendor-patched/blitz-dom-0.3.0-beta.4 commit

# Write the series back out:
pnpm run vendor:regen                 # all crates
pnpm run vendor:regen -- blitz-dom    # one crate only

# Review and commit (in the kitesurf repo):
git diff -- scripts/patches/
```

Keep vendor-tree commits **atomic** — each becomes one numbered patch
in the series, and the series IS the reviewable delta we ship (and the
unit we'd upstream). Amending/squashing/reordering with `git rebase -i
vendor-base` is fine; regen renumbers the files.

`vendor:regen` refuses to run with uncommitted changes in the vendor
tree (uncommitted work can't be attributed to a patch). It runs
`git format-patch --zero-commit --no-signature -N vendor-base..HEAD`,
then **round-trip verifies**: a scratch repo is rebuilt from the
freshly-written series and diffed recursively against your tree —
any mismatch aborts non-zero. A successful regen is a guarantee that
the committed series reproduces exactly what you tested.

Note: the materialiser caches by series sha8. Editing any `.patch`
invalidates the cache and the next `vendor:apply` / `build:wasm`
re-materialises (wiping the repo, including unregenerated local
commits). Regen refreshes the stamp after writing, so the normal
edit → commit → regen loop keeps your repo (and its reflog) intact.
Run `vendor:regen` before any operation that might wipe the tree
(e.g. `rm -rf packages/core/target`).

## Bumping a vendor crate

When upstream releases a new version we want:

1. `cargo update -p parley` (or whichever crate) from the repo root
   to refresh the root `Cargo.lock` against the registry.
2. Rename the series dir to the new version, e.g.
   `git mv scripts/patches/parley-0.12.0 scripts/patches/parley-0.12.1`,
   and update the `CRATES` array in
   `scripts/get-patched-vendor-crates.mjs` plus the path in
   the repo-root `Cargo.toml`'s `[patch.crates-io]` block.
3. Run `pnpm run vendor:apply`. The series either applies cleanly (no
   further action needed) or `git am` stops at the first rejecting
   patch with the offending hunk on stderr.
4. For a rejected patch, resolve in the materialised repo like any
   `git am` conflict: `git apply --reject` the failed patch, hand-merge
   the `.rej` files, `git add -A`, `git am --continue` (repeat until
   the series lands), then `pnpm run vendor:regen -- <crate>` to write
   the rebased series back.
5. Check whether upstream absorbed any of our patches — if a commit
   becomes empty on the new base, drop it (note it in the kitesurf
   commit message) rather than shipping a no-op patch.
6. Update the provenance table above.
7. Smoke: `pnpm run test:e2e lifecycle-demo`, which builds from the
   regenerated series.

---

## Why this approach

- **Visibility**: the in-tree delta is small, and `git log` in any
  materialised tree tells the story commit by commit — subject, body,
  author, date. `git diff scripts/patches/` still shows the entire
  set of upstream modifications at a glance.
- **Incrementality**: one logical change = one commit = one patch
  file. Review, revert, and upstream each independently instead of
  re-reading one ever-growing monolithic diff.
- **No vendored bulk**: we don't commit pristine upstream source we
  don't own. The patch series replaced 2.6 MB of vendored source.
- **Cache by series sha**: changing any patch invalidates the matching
  materialised tree and, because the patch files are inputs of Bazel's
  patched crate repositories, the Bazel build of that crate.
- **Direct cargo still works**: `[patch.crates-io]` points at a stable
  in-tree path (`packages/core/target/vendor-patched/<crate>-<version>`),
  so `cargo build` from `packages/core/` works as long as the
  materialiser has run at least once since the last series change.
- **Each tree is its own cargo workspace**: the materialiser stamps an
  empty `[workspace]` table into the vendor-base commit, because the
  repo-root workspace's walk-up would otherwise claim the tree as a
  stray member (`workspace.exclude` can't cover the versioned paths).

## Why not contribute upstream

We will. Several fixes are marked "should land upstream" in their
commit messages (stylo invalidation, boa_ast scope analysis, boa_gc
worklist). The per-commit series makes that mechanical: each patch is
already a self-contained commit with rationale, ready to cherry-pick
onto an upstream clone. The parley inline-decoration work goes as a
follow-up to linebender/parley#208 ("Tracking: Features for Blitz")
with the algorithm spelled out in a design doc.
